question: According to HSBC's 2023 Annual Report and Accounts: Analyze how the Group’s accounting classifications for debt instruments affect the reporting of unrealised losses and capital in a rising interest rate environment, and explain why these losses may reverse over time.

For hold-to-collect-and-sell positions, changes in fair value are recognised in equity through OCI rather than in profit or loss. For hold-to-collect instruments measured at amortised cost, there is a cumulative unrealised loss of $1.7bn that is not reflected on the balance sheet at all; this included $1.0bn of debt instruments held to manage interest rate exposure, which improved by $0.8bn in 2023. Over time, these adverse fair value movements tend to unwind as the instruments approach maturity, because the contractual cash flows are ultimately collected and the temporary fair value fluctuation reverses. However, the text also cautions that not all such instruments will necessarily be held to maturity. Overall, the Group is positively exposed to rising interest rates through net interest income, but the accounting treatment of hold-to-collect-and-sell instruments can create an early-stage capital drag that is expected to diminish over time.
